To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the most accurate Type 1 error rates are found for two product methods (the product of the independent variable with the product method and the product of the independent variables with a product of the coefficients method) and the difference-in-coeffients methods (the difference between two regression coefficients and the difference between the regression coefficients with the independent variable and the intervening variable as the independent variable).

(a) the test of the significance of the product of two coefficients (the product method) and the difference-in-coeffients method (the difference-in-coefficents method) have the most accurate type I error rates and highest statistical power except in one important case in which type I error rates are inflated, and (b) the test of significance of the two coefficients jointly (the joint significance test) has the most accurate type 1 error rates and highest power across all cases.

(1) the test of the significance of the product of the two regression coefficients comprising the intervening variable (IV) effect has low statistical power and (2) two methods based on the difference between the two regression coefficients have the most accurate statistical properties across a wide variety of situations, although one of them is too liberal when the effect of the IV on the mediator is small.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a class of statistical models in which the effect of an explanatory variable on a response variable is transmitted through the effect of an intervening variable.
the effects of the independent and intervening variables on the dependent variable and the statistical significance of these effects.

the problem of how to test the significance of the effect of a mediator (i.e., intervening variable) on a dependent variable, given the effect of an antecedent variable on the mediator and the effect of the antecedent variable (direct effect) on the dependent variable.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Baron and Kenny approach is not recommended.
the test of the intervening variable is the joint significance of two regression coefficients.

the Baron-Kenny test is not recommended, that the 2 difference-in coefficients tests have the highest power and lowest Type I error rate in most cases, that the joint significance test of the two effects has the highest statistical power and lowest Type 1 error rate in the most important case, and that the 2 methods based on the product of coefficients are the best overall.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Baron and Kenny (1986), Sobel (1982), and the product-of-coefficient methods have the best Type I error rates.
the best methods are the 2 difference-incoefficients methods, the 2 tests based on the distribution for the product, and the test of the 2 effects that comprise the intervening variable effect.

the best methods for testing the statistical significance of an intervening variable effect are those that test the joint significance of all effects that comprise the intervening variable effect, including tests based on the joint significance of 2 regression coefficients, the joint significance of a regression coefficient and the product of 2 regression residuals, the joint significance test of the regression coefficient of the product of a standardized independent variable and standardized intervening variable, and the joint significance of an unstandardized intervening variable effect, an unstandardized independent variable effect
